summary: On Saturday morning, MS NOW journalists were denied access to the White House grounds, a day after President Donald Trump announced a ban on the network, CNN, and Politico citing "fake news."
The White House began enforcing the "ban" Trump declared "effective immediately" on Friday, though journalists from the affected outlets remained on the complex through that evening.
MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Gardner said an officer disabled her badge upon arrival, forcing her to report live from outside the perimeter after being denied entry.
Protesting the exclusion, the network released a statement Saturday asserting the White House belongs to the American people and intending to defend its First Amendment rights.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will meet Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on Sunday at JPMorgan Chase headquarters in New York to discuss AI security, trade, and economic issues.

title: Trump says he will create 'AI Force,' name AI czar

summary: On Friday, President Donald Trump announced a security agreement with Denmark and Greenland granting Washington expanded military access while preserving Danish sovereignty over the Arctic territory.

Under the deal, the U.S. gains permanent overflight and basing rights, while explicitly banning non-NATO nations from establishing military installations or making sensitive investments in Greenland.

The framework strengthens common Arctic security for NATO allies while de-escalating tensions that previously strained relations, reaffirming Greenland's right to self-determination within the Danish Kingdom.
title: US, Denmark reach deal giving US ‘permanent security control’ over Greenland

Since the Trump administration and Israel initiated the Iran war on Feb 28, the Pentagon's Defense Casualty Analysis System lists 18 fatalities. Officials note internal records show higher numbers because some deaths involved personnel in the region during hostilities.

As of Friday, 14 fatalities are listed under Operation Epic Fury, with four categorized under Overseas Operations. Officials familiar with the Defense Department's internal accounting data noted the public database excludes several deaths occurring in the region.

Officials expressed frustration with the lack of transparency, citing that proper accounting remains critical for families receiving survivor benefits, which depend on whether deaths occurred during official duties.

title: US troop deaths in Iran war exceed Pentagon count by at least four, Washington Post reports

summary: On Friday, Warren Buffett announced he is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, with his son Howard Buffett replacing him as chairman while Buffett becomes chairman emeritus and remains a director.

Under Buffett's tenure since 1965, the firm transformed from a failed New England textiles mill into a $1 trillion conglomerate with $44.5 billion in operating earnings and nearly 400,000 employees.

title: Warren Buffett Steps Down as Berkshire Hathaway Chairman

summary: On Saturday, a NORAD F-16 fighter jet intercepted a general aviation aircraft that violated restricted airspace over Camp David while President Donald Trump was visiting the Maryland retreat.

To gain the pilot's attention, the NORAD pilot deployed flares, which pose no danger to the ground. Intercepted pilots must tune to 121.5 or 243.0 and reverse course immediately.

title: US F-16 intercepts aircraft over restricted airspace near Camp David

President Xi Jinping made energy self-reliance a cornerstone of China's latest five-year plan to shield against foreign supply disruptions, which former senior CIA analyst Jonathan Czin called "a vindication of Xi's last five-year plan and his focus on self-reliance."

Energy analysts credit Beijing's slashing imports to 8.1 million barrels per day with moderating global prices, as Michael Lynch, president of Strategic Energy and Economic Research, noted China "didn't panic and by turning to their inventories they kept the price down for everybody."

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington next week amid diplomatic tensions, as President Trump prepares to meet Gulf Cooperation Council leaders Tuesday in New York; the Trump administration has urged Beijing to press Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, though Chinese officials oppose the U.S. war.

Bank of America analysts forecast oil at $83 a barrel for the second half of the year but warn prices could spike to $150 if violence escalates, as Iran-backed militias attacked this month, Saudi Arabia shut a Red Sea pipeline, and Yemen-based Houthis seized strategic islands to disrupt shipping.
title: China’s Oil Stockpile Helps Curb Price Spike During Iran War

summary: On Friday, the NAACP and other civil rights groups sued the Trump administration, seeking to block potential deployment of federal agents at polling places during November's midterm elections, alleging voter intimidation violations.

The lawsuit follows the Trump administration's recently expanded efforts to identify noncitizens registered to vote, despite no evidence of widespread voter fraud. President Donald Trump and senior officials have not ruled out deploying federal agents to polling places.

Plaintiffs argue these actions violate Section 11 of the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits voter intimidation. The lawsuit states voters, particularly Black, Latino, and Asian voters, are afraid to participate in civic life, constituting unlawful intimidation.

Mullin claimed ICE would only be at polling places if responding to threats or serving warrants, though the administration has not ruled out broader deployments. FBI Director Kash Patel refused to confirm or deny polling-site plans earlier this week.

This marks at least the second lawsuit challenging potential polling-site deployments, following a similar action filed last week by the City of Denver and civil rights groups. Federal law bars armed officers from polling locations, and Section 11 remains legally intact despite earlier Supreme Court weakening of the broader Voting Rights Act.
title: NAACP sues to block Trump administration from sending armed agents to polls

summary: On September 24, President Donald Trump will host a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping, with tech executives including Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Tim Cook, Jensen Huang, Sundar Pichai, and Jeff Bezos expected to attend.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng will meet in New York on September 20 to discuss AI safety. Bessent has signaled openness to exploring shared risks around the technology.

Trump has rejected calls for domestic AI regulation, arguing the United States must maintain supremacy over China in the technology race. Altman will brief the United Nations Security Council next week regarding international coordination.
title: Elon Musk, Sam Altman Among AI Giants Invited to Trump-Xi State Dinner

title: UN allows Palestinian president to again speak via video after US denies visa

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the temporary FBI -Canada cooperation pause as Patel’s “petty move,” “tantrum,” or anger-driven overreaction, even calling him “unfit,” while right-leaning accounts emphasize CBC’s “refusal” to use “terrorism” without attribution and label its guidance a “controversial directive,” portraying Patel’s response as a consequential institutional “freeze.” The pivotal divide is whether the dispute reflects reckless retaliation or justified resistance to politically cautious language about 9/11; left coverage stresses that cooperation continued in some areas, whereas the right foregrounds “frozen” ties.
Center coverage largely uses “paused” and narrates the sequence without evaluative language.

All perspectives agree the action was temporary, involved Kash Patel and the RCMP, and arose from CBC’s 9/11 policy, reflecting wider clashes over media norms, national security, and institutional authority.
summary: FBI Director Kash Patel temporarily halted some cooperation with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police earlier this month after objecting to a Canadian Broadcasting Corporation memo discouraging journalists from labeling the September 11 attacks as "terrorism" without attribution.

Ahead of the 9/11 anniversary, an internal CBC memo reminded journalists to attribute the term "terrorism" to experts, prompting international criticism before the network reversed its editorial guidance on August 28.

Patel escalated tensions on X, threatening that Canadian agencies refusing to reject the guidance would "no longer have friend in this FBI," while characterizing the policy as a "bastardization of history."

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police stated it maintains "strong relationships" with allies, and the FBI's disruption of meetings appears to have been short-lived, ending around the 25th anniversary of the attacks.
title: FBI Temporarily Halted Cooperation with Canada

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the reported passage of over 1 billion barrels and 18 million barrels in one day as evidence that U.S. protection is “paying off” and “momentum is building,” while casting the operation as a coercive “blockade” and warning of “annihilation.” Right-leaning coverage turns the same figures into an “ironclad blockade,” “success,” and Iran ’s “zero” exports, portraying U.S. control and Iranian defeat; one outlet even attacks the commander as a “terrorist.” Center coverage stays comparatively restrained, calling it a “significant milestone.” All repeat CENTCOM’s claims, but diverge over intervention, credibility, and geopolitical victory.
summary: Oil and liquefied natural gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz reached a six-month high in the past two weeks, with Admiral Brad Cooper crediting U.S. naval protection and mine clearance efforts as "paying off."

Energy Secretary Chris Wright noted on September 13 that markets rely on roughly 10 million barrels daily transiting the Strait, a critical dependency the President Donald Trump administration has emphasized amid soaring fuel prices in an election year.

Persian Gulf allies shipped more than one billion barrels of crude through the waterway in the last couple of months, while Cooper stated "Clearly, momentum is building" regarding collaborative efforts with insurers and shipping companies.

Saudi authorities issued two early-morning air raid alerts for Riyadh on September 19, the first since March and April, following a September 17 Houthi strike in Taif that caused casualties and disrupted alternative routes.

Regional negotiations on shipping routes have faltered, while Iran claims it "has exported zero barrels" under the U.S.-enforced blockade, underscoring persistent geopolitical tensions affecting long-term maritime stability.
title: US military says over 1B barrels of oil shipped through Strait of Hormuz under US blockade
topic_full: Oil and Gas Sector · United States

bias: Coverage diverges mainly by emphasis, not overt partisanship: the left foregrounds Judge George H.
Wu’s “won’t lift” stance, continued oversight under Musical.ly’s 2019 consent decree, and the conditional $100 million beyond the immediate $300 million payment.

Center coverage stresses children’s privacy, a settlement “hurdle,” and “uncertainty” for TikTok ’s U.S. operations, while the right largely repeats the restrained “signals rejection” formulation, de-emphasizing background and implications.
All perspectives place the proposed $400 million agreement and partial judicial rejection at the center, revealing selective framing rather than genuine ideological polarization.
summary: On Friday, District Judge George H. Wu tentatively rejected a request to lift the 2019 consent decree on TikTok , maintaining federal oversight of the app's privacy practices.

The Federal Trade Commission originally imposed this decree in 2019 after settling a $5.7m children's privacy case with Musical.ly, the predecessor to TikTok, requiring record-keeping obligations through 2029.
Under the $400 million settlement announced in August, ByteDance agreed to pay $300 million immediately, with an additional $100m contingent on the court terminating the decree.

Judge George wrote that the court "cannot determine that it constitutes a durable remedy", tentatively denying the request because termination was not suitably tailored to the asserted change in circumstance.
In contrast to the US process, The European Commission is increasing supervision under the Digital Services Act, accusing TikTok of addictive design rather than removing oversight.
title: US judge signals rejection of part of TikTok privacy settlement

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the lawsuits as “a fresh legal fight,” stressing intergenerational trauma, ethical accountability, and the moral force of “Nazi-looted” art , including Lucas Cranach the Elder’s *Adam and Eve* at the Norton Simon Museum.

Right-Leaning coverage foregrounds restitution, unresolved ownership, and Dina Gottliebova Babbitt’s coerced Auschwitz watercolors, invoking “persecution, coercion and genocide” and Mengele’s “Angel of Death” epithet.
Center coverage de-emphasizes personal histories, emphasizing California and federal legal changes and the first claims filed under them.
Across perspectives, Jewish heirs or Holocaust-victim representatives challenge holdings at Norton Simon and Auschwitz museums over Nazi-era seizures.
summary: On Monday, two lawsuits were filed in Los Angeles seeking return of Nazi-looted art . The Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles sued Norton Simon Museum for Lucas Cranach paintings, while Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt's daughters sued the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial and Museum for watercolors.

California and Congress recently enacted legislation, including the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025, to remove procedural barriers that have prevented families from recovering art stolen by the Nazi regime. These laws ensure restitution claims are decided on their merits.

The Jewish Federation seeks Lucas Cranach's 'Adam and Eve,' which Norton Simon Museum claims it purchased legally in the 1960s. Babbitt's daughters demand return of seven watercolors she was forced to paint for Nazi physician Josef Mengele while imprisoned at Auschwitz.

Museums maintain they hold legal titles to the works. The Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial argues the watercolors are essential historical documents of Mengele's crimes, while Norton Simon Foundation claims prior judicial rulings established the museum's rightful ownership of the Cranach paintings.

These cases test whether new statutes can overcome decades of possession and legal barriers. With over 600,000 works stolen by the Nazis remaining unrestituted, the lawsuits represent a pivotal moment for Holocaust-era restitution policy.
title: Los Angeles Lawsuits Seek Return of Auschwitz Watercolors and Cranach Paintings

bias: Left-Leaning framing casts Brian Fitzpatrick’s repeated “distancing” from Trump as an urgent, possibly futile defense against a liability, emphasizing Trump’s “low approval ratings,” rising gas prices, and electoral vulnerability.

Right-Leaning framing likewise stresses that separation “may not save him,” but foregrounds voter discontent with Trump’s “crass style” and “chaotic approach to governing,” without the left’s economic-Democratic strategy.
Center coverage adds Mary Ryan’s reconsideration and Fitzpatrick’s Iran war-powers vote.

Yet the three versions largely reproduce the same account, agreeing on Fitzpatrick’s independence, convention absence, and uncertain reelection prospects—differences reflecting emphasis more than fundamentally distinct narratives.
summary: In the competitive 1st Congressional District, five-term Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick is working to distance himself from President Donald Trump while facing a challenge from Democratic commissioner Bob Harvie.
Voters like Mary Ryan plan to support Harvie this November, citing frustration with Trump's influence over Congress and a belief that Fitzpatrick remains too aligned with his party's leadership.

Fitzpatrick has disbursed nearly $5 million in campaign funds, utilizing negative attack ads against Harvie, while arguing on a podcast with Rep. Tom Suozzi that citizens are "sick and tired of the noise."
Harvie denies claims that he is under FBI investigation, filing a federal defamation lawsuit against a super PAC running attack ads while emphasizing his deep local roots as a candidate advantage.

Political science professor Robert Speel notes that while Democrats label Fitzpatrick as vulnerable every two years, he consistently wins, though voter defections could threaten the Republican Party's narrow U.S. House majority.
title: Fitzpatrick Distances Himself From Trump in Competitive Pennsylvania Race

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames funding shortfalls as an urgent voting-access threat, using phrases like “sound alarm,” “racial justice,” and “depress turnout,” while de-emphasizing the broader power struggle.

Right-Leaning coverage portrays “liberal voter groups” that “scramble” after donors “pull back,” stressing organizational weakness, “robust voter protection,” and risks to communities of color and civil-rights groups.
Center coverage adds that control of Congress—and the remainder of Trump’s term—is at stake, while qualifying claims with “could” and attribution.

The pivotal divide is whether the shortfall signals an equity-driven participation crisis or donor-driven partisan fragility; all emphasize staffing cuts, midterm timing, and possible turnout effects.
summary: As midterm voting begins, major progressive voter engagement and racial justice organizations face steep funding shortfalls and staffing cutbacks, threatening voter mobilization efforts critical to controlling Congress under President Donald.

Following the 2024 election, wealthy donors have tightened purse strings, with some fearing retribution from the administration; Tameka Ramsey-Brown of the Michigan Coalition reported donors asked to remove "Black" from its name to avoid attention.

America Votes executive director Daria Dawson says the hub has fallen "well below" 2022 funding levels, while Vamos a Votar requires $5.4 million to fund turnout across 10 states and 17 House districts, with fundraising trailing 2018 cycles by nearly 40%.

To counter shortfalls, groups are increasing reliance on artificial intelligence and ride-sharing partnerships to boost turnout; The Democratic National Committee spokesperson Angelo Fern said the party is making "historic investments" in its own infrastructure.

The Supreme Court gutted the 1965 Voting Rights Act this year, complicating mobilization efforts; Esosa Osa of Onyx Impact described the donor retreat as "handcuffing" ability to persuade voters, saying "We are watching surrender, not strategy.
title: Progressive Voter Groups Face Funding Shortfalls as Midterm Voting Begins

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the dispute through everyday “ privacy rights,” using the dismissive “haul... ass” to cast Hawley’s intervention as theatrical; center coverage emphasizes alleged “abuse,” “unauthorized tracking,” and Wyden and Schiff’s concerns about reproductive-health and immigration searches.

Right-Leaning coverage broadens the threat into “mass surveillance,” a “sprawling network,” and possible false accusations, while portraying Hawley as a “leading critic” and the Senate as ready to “grill” CEOs.
The pivotal divide is whether scrutiny centers on partisan performance, sensitive misuse, or nationwide technological overreach.
All perspectives, however, stress congressional testimony and privacy risks, reflecting wider arguments over civil liberties, policing, and government power.
summary: On Friday, Senator Josh Hawley invited CEOs from Flock Safety, Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions, and Verkada to testify on Wednesday, September 23, 2026, regarding mass surveillance systems.

The investigation follows widespread reports of police misusing surveillance technology to stalk women and conduct unauthorized tracking. Senator Ron Wyden demanded answers regarding privacy protections.

Hawley noted that AI-powered cameras capture 20 billion snapshots of cars monthly across a network of more than 120,000 devices. At least 50 law enforcement officers have been charged for illegal use.

Verkada CEO Filip Kaliszan will not attend, though his company is providing information to the subcommittee. It remains unclear if other invited CEOs, including Flock CEO Garrett Langley, will appear.

Congress must draft legislation to protect Americans' privacy, Hawley emphasized, arguing that safeguards should not depend on corporate policies but rather on rules enduring beyond current executive tenures.
title: Hawley Calls Flock, Axon, Motorola CEOs to Senate Hearing on Surveillance

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Tahir Ali’s “military action” remarks as renewed advocacy to “protect Palestinians,” stressing his call for both Hamas and Israel to disarm and his earlier support for deploying troops.

Right-Leaning accounts intensify the wording into “war” or “invade,” foreground his Muslim identity, condemn the alleged comparison as a “grotesque equivalence” or “Jew-hating,” and emphasize his “unreserved” apology and Labour warning.

Both retain the parliamentary context, though the exact meaning of “military action” remains unclear, and both highlight disarmament and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict—revealing a broader divide over intervention, proportionality, and identity-driven interpretations.
summary: Labour MP Tahir Ali apologized on Wednesday after calling for British "military action" against Israel during a House of Commons debate on Monday, receiving a formal warning from the Labour Party's chief whip.
Ali intervened while Liberal Democrat MP Richard Foord argued Hamas must disarm as part of a lasting settlement, leading Ali to question why disarmament demands were confined to Hamas.
Characterizing Israel as responsible for "genocide" and "ethnic cleansing," Ali cited historical British military interventions in Iraq and Syria as precedent for action.
Israeli Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli criticized Ali's remarks, while the British government rejected the proposal, focusing on pressing for a ceasefire and securing hostage returns.

Monday's debate exposed deeper parliamentary divisions, with Labour MP Imran Hussain calling for an end to arms sales to Israel while Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty emphasized Britain's ongoing "important security, intelligence and defense relationship" with Israel.
title: British MP Apologizes After Calling for 'Military Action' Against Israel

summary: On Tuesday, The International Civil Liberties Monitoring Group released a report warning of a "near-total absence" of effective recourse for organizations facing de-banking due to alleged ties to terrorist financing.

The report argues de-banking is a predictable outcome of Canada's anti-terror financing framework, with Muslim-led charities and NGOs operating in Syria, Palestine, or Pakistan facing disproportionate impacts.
In one instance, a humanitarian organization operating in Syria received 15 to 30 days' notice before losing services, yet "No explanation of the underlying risk was given."
Financial institutions face no legal requirement to explain account closures, and no independent body in Canada reviews whether derisking decisions are non-discriminatory or evidence-based.
The group issued a dozen recommendations for structural reform and transparency; Tim McSorley, the monitoring group's national coordinator, said "We need to see concrete policy changes.
title: Action needed to ensure groups aren't unduly 'de-banked' over terror risks: report

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Trump’s attack as an emotional outburst, using “wails” and quotation marks around “trillions” to signal skepticism, while right-leaning coverage presents a forceful challenge to an obstructive Court, using “unloaded,” “no courage,” “wrecked,” and “they blinked,” and emphasizing legal defeats for trade and immigration.

The pivotal divides are the Court’s limits on tariffs and birthright- citizenship policy, plus whether losses amounted to “billions” or “trillions.” Center coverage uses “blasts” and attributes the contested figure without endorsing it.
Across perspectives, the dispute remains a clash over presidential power, judicial authority, economic stakes, and immigration.
summary: On Saturday, President Donald Trump criticized the Supreme Court for issuing "faulty, political, and ridiculous decisions" on tariffs and Birthright Citizenship, claiming these rulings cost the United States "trillions of dollars."

The criticism stems from two major defeats: the February ruling blocking broad tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the June decision upholding Birthright Citizenship protections under the Fourteenth Amendment.

Writing on Truth Social, Trump argued the court "lacked the Courage to MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN," despite the conservative majority including his appointees Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett.

Earlier this month, District Judge Deborah Boardman blocked a new administration order attempting to restrict Birthright Citizenship, finding the government cannot deny citizenship to children the Supreme Court deemed citizens at birth.

Allies continue discussing ways to keep the debate alive through future litigation, legislation, and judicial nominations, though The White House has not indicated whether Trump is pursuing additional legal or legislative remedies.
title: President Trump Attacks Supreme Court Over Tariff and Birthright Citizenship Rulings

summary: Virginia Democratic lawmakers advanced a constitutional amendment protecting abortion -related decisions for the November ballot.
Abortion is currently legal in Virginia through 26 weeks and six days, but the state constitution does not explicitly protect abortion rights.
Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Attorney General Jay Jones support the measure, while Catholic leaders urge voters to reject it.
Bishop Michael Burbidge said the amendment could threaten women’s health, unborn life, and parental rights.
title: Virginia Democrats Push Constitutional Right to Abortion as Catholic Leaders Mobilize Against Measure

bias: The left-leaning framing foregrounds accountability, using phrases such as “hit with,” “claims,” “spurs,” and “watchdog complaint” to cast Trump’s “my money” assertion as potentially conflicting with restrictions on officeholders directing super PAC funds.
Center-Leaning coverage softens that edge, presenting the same claim as “raising questions” and connecting the dispute to the 2026 midterms.
Both highlight MAGA Inc.’s roughly $400 million, the FEC complaint, and the legal limits, while treating alleged illegality as an allegation—not proof of wrongdoing.
With no right-leaning headlines provided, and largely shared underlying reporting, the ideological divide appears limited; the main tension is scrutiny versus political context.
summary: The Campaign Legal Center filed a formal complaint this week with the Federal Election Commission, alleging President Donald Trump's control over the $400 million super PAC MAGA Inc. violates federal law.
Federal law prohibits officeholders from directing spending for groups without contribution limits, yet Trump has repeatedly stated he maintains control over MAGA Inc. and its financial decisions.
Saurav Ghosh, director of federal campaign finance reform at the Campaign Legal Center, called the arrangement a "clear violation" of the law, citing Trump's remark: "Let's do this, let's do that."
MAGA Inc. spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer dismissed the complaint as "frivolous," while the Federal Election Commission remains unable to act because its board lacks enough confirmed members to meet.
As of Thursday, MAGA Inc. and allied super PACs reserved nearly $140 million nationwide, including $10 million already spent on the Texas Senate race.
title: Trump Calling MAGA Inc. Funds ‘My Money’ Spurs FEC Complaint
